#2038. Manchester United’s attack may be their best form of defence this season

Is attack going to be Manchester United’s best form of defence this season?

There was plenty to like going forward, particularly once United had nudged their way in front after their second lucky break of what had hitherto looked like being a tricky afternoon.

Give this team a little space and they have the attacking players to inflict some serious damage, none more so than Bruno Fernandes who, just five days after collecting the PFA Players’ Player of the Year award, scored a hat-trick in what was another inspired performance.

Ipswich Town will testify to that after a sobering second half when it felt like United were going to score with every raid forward and, for a time, even threaten to equal the nine goals they scored against the promoted side at this ground 31 years ago.

In the returning Marcus Rashford, whom manager Michael Carrick likened to a “new signing”, Matheus Cunha, Bryan Mbeumo and, of course, Fernandes, United have an intriguing blend of attacking players. Throw in Kobbie Mainoo who, on another day, would have stolen the headlines with an imperious display in central midfield, and one thing United are not lacking for is creativity.

Their offensive problems tend to come when opponents sit in and ask to be broken down. Hull City, of course, proved as much last weekend when United looked desperately short of ideas in attack.

But you would probably bet on Carrick being more likely to find solutions to that particular conundrum than some of the defensive headaches that again reared their head here.

A week after that shock 2-0 defeat to Hull, United were given another scare when Ipswich took advantage of more meek defending to lead and could easily have scored more in that first half.

With a couple of days of the transfer window still remaining, it would feel remiss of United not to add a quality left-back before the deadline passes.

Those 15 minutes in the first half when Abdul Fatawu gave Luke Shaw a torrid time, not least in that moment he raced away from the United defender to cross for Leif Davis to score, should tell United’s hierarchy everything about the risks of not reinforcing in the position.

Ipswich STUN Old Trafford! Leif Davis does superbly to volley past Senne Lammens and give Gary O'Neil's side the lead 💥 pic.twitter.com/sJ0XNf8OiT

Defensive rebuilding is next summer’s big project but some things cannot wait and that is before we get to some of the issues in the other full-back position, which Ipswich also exploited. Fatawu aside, Daizen Maeda and Davis caused Diogo Dalot and Mbeumo problems down United’s right and the excellent Julio Enciso was a persistent nuisance until the game fell away from Ipswich.

For all the defensive concerns, though, United were exhilarating going forward, especially once they found themselves in front after benefiting from a curious ruling that dictated Harry Maguire’s “accidental” handball in the lead-up to the home team’s second goal was “not punishable” because he did not end up scoring.

In other words, had Maguire himself found the net and not seen his cross-cum-shot deflect in off the Ipswich defender Jacob Greaves, the goal would not have stood.

Harry Maguire's shot cannons in off Jacob Greaves and Manchester United are in front at Old Trafford after a VAR review! 💪 pic.twitter.com/hUdogDQX6k

United were brilliant from that point on. There had been flashes of the threat they hold in the opening 45 minutes but thereafter Ipswich just found themselves routinely bludgeoned and unable to escape the tailspin. As the rain poured down, the goals poured in. Gary O’Neil, the Ipswich manager, talked about a lack of “emotional discipline” but plenty of teams would have found United hard to contain in that moment.

Rashford was a threat on his first start for United for 626 days. Harness his talent in the right way and he will be an enormous asset. Cunha’s withdrawn role, with Fernandes and Mbeumo routinely racing in behind United’s false nine, caused Ipswich no end of problems. Amad Diallo and Mason Mount were missing through injury and Benjamin Sesko, a substitute, is still working his way back to fitness after missing all of pre-season. Patrick Dorgu almost scored a couple after coming on. So Carrick has plenty of options.

Fernandes was at his irrepressible best, initially punishing poor Marcelino Núñez after his slip allowed Cunha to play in the United captain to equalise five minutes before the restart and then taking the game away from Ipswich in the second.

Bruno Fernandes equalises for Manchester United! 🔴 pic.twitter.com/CdEI1REeUD

After missing two penalties in pre-season, he made no mistake from the spot after Greaves had brought down Cunha. He then steered home a close-range finish after Mbeumo’s shot was blocked and almost lobbed the Ipswich goalkeeper Kjell Scherpen from 60 yards. His last act was to send Mbeumo through to score with a delicious lob.

"He's the prince of this place!"Bruno Fernandes completes his hat-trick 🎩 pic.twitter.com/KgLlaMcKGR

This was the first time United had scored five goals in a Premier League game since beating Leeds United five years ago and you had to go back 10 years to find the last time they had more shots in a league match.

“There was a good mixture [in attack] there,” Carrick said. “Obviously we’ve got to find the right balance and options. We can play slightly different ways across the front line and a lot of the front players can play different roles.

“It was a little bit different today playing Cunha a bit deeper, and Bryan and Marcus a little bit higher. So it’s up to us to try and get that balance right, but certainly there’s creation and there’s goals within the squad, for sure.”

There was little doubt United benefited from the return of Mainoo in midfield. Summer signing Andrey Santos was the one to make way and Mainoo in turn produced the kind of intelligent, inventive display alongside Youri Tielemans that makes you wonder how Thomas Tuchel did not give the midfielder a minute for England at this summer’s World Cup.

He recycles possession beautifully, excels in the tight spaces, has a nose for goal and an eye for a pass and a lovely ability to glide past players even though he is not quick. Ipswich could not live with him.

Asked where Mainoo could still develop, Carrick said, half in jest: “On today’s performance, not much, really. I thought he was pretty much all-around, very, very good for a first start back. I understand Bruno will get a lot of credit today, and he deserves that as well, but I thought Kobbie was immense in the middle of the pitch for us and underpinned the performance of the team.”

The Man Utd head coach told Sky Sports: “It was a good win. It was a really good win in the end. We played some really good football. The biggest thing today was the mentality of the boys tp overcomes setbacks. We’re going to have them and it depends on how you deal with them. I was really pleased with that. It’s easy to look at the result but the mentality and the stubbornness really pleased me.

“We controlled the game pretty well for the most part. A lot of our play was looking on the way to how we wanted it to look. The boys took it on really well and we were fabulous.”

And on Bruno Fernandes, Carrick added: “He showed his quality today. Bruno did what he’s good at. He’s had a big week winning awards. Three goals and a fantastic performance.

“There were a lot of positives with and without the ball but it’s the whole mentality dealing with it and trusting each other. Last week didn’t go for us and we accept that. Today was a lot better.

“We’re not getting carried away. We were down last week but everything wasn’t wrong. We can still get better, we haven’t cracked it. We’ll get ready for the next.”

Speaking with Sky Sports, he said: “Really unlucky to be 2-1 down, really unlucky - two of the most unlucky goals you will see, but then not good enough to get back into it. We got punished by a very good side.

“To beat Manchester United at Old Trafford you need the moments to go in your favour and they didn’t. Rules can go against you, or a deflection, there are lots of things that can happen in a game that are beyond your control.

“It is a complicated rule - handball if it’s the goal scorer but not if it takes a deflection and was heading off the target. I think that is tough for a referee.

“But no problem. I’m not here to moan about refs. We get no points, at Old Trafford a lot of people leave with no points but we leave with an understanding of where to get better.

“We have three points from two tough games. A good start for us. It is the Premier League, the lads understand there will be highs and lows. We don’t want there to be too many lows but the lads are fine in there. They understand.”

This time, Gary O’Neil is the boss and they’ve already ticked off one victory thanks to those three points against Sunderland.

Is he the man to guide Ipswich to safety?

Ipswich enjoyed a great start back in the top flight by winning their opening game against Sunderland and will be out to build on that victory.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of Sunday’s late Premier League kick-off between Manchester United and Ipswich Town at Old Trafford.

Man Utd suffered an almighty upset last weekend as they slumped to a shock 2-0 defeat against Hull City in Yorkshire. The hosts scored twice after 38 minutes, leaving Michael Carrick’s men with a mountain to climb, but they simply had no answer so Man Utd were shambolic defensively and toothless in attack.

When the fixture list was released, everyone looked at Man Utd’s opening two games against newly-promoted sides as the ideal opportunity for maximum points. But now, there is serious pressure on today’s home team to deliver in front of their fans.

Reflecting on last week’s loss in a press conference ahead of this outing, Carrick said: “I think your success comes from how well you deal with setbacks in the end. In any position, or certainly any sport, particularly this one, going through a season, there are going to be setbacks, sometimes a bit smaller than others. It’s how you deal with that initially, how you react to it and what comes next. I think that ultimately decides what type of team you’re going to become.

“So far, we’ve dealt with those setbacks really well within games and game to game. We had one last week, there’s no getting away from it, and it’s disappointing, but we’re looking to bounce back. We’ve had a good week. The boys have re-focused, learnt from where we could have improved and kept pushing forward.”

Against the odds, Ipswich began their 2026-27 Premier League campaign with a 2-1 comeback victory over Sunderland, with summer signing Emersonn equalising before substitute Jack Clarke found a 90th-minute winner at Portman Road. They followed this game with another triumph at home in midweek, beating Leicester City 3-1 in the League Cup second round.

With all eyes on Man Utd after their stuttering start, Ipswich will see this as an ideal opportunity to ruffle the feathers of a Premier League heavyweight and further dent their sky-high ambitions.

#2037. Femi Seriki in Sheffield United contract limbo - Birmingham City & Southampton must plot moves

Sheffield United endured a tough summer window and a subsequent tough start to the 2026/27 Championship campaign, but it appears as though head coach Chris Wilder has got the club back on track and looking up instead of over their shoulder.

Sheffield United saw each of Callum O'Hare, Gustavo Hamer, and Andre Brooks leave Bramall Lane over the summer, and with parachute payments running out, the Blades could only rely upon free agents and loans for their replacements.

Unsurprisingly, things began poorly, as heading into the first international break, head coach Wilder was under severe pressure, having just been knocked out of the EFL Cup at the hands of League Two Fleetwood Town, who themselves would go on to defeat Arsenal.

However, since that break, Sheffield United have won five, drawn once, and lost twice, and as a result, are within touching distance of the play-offs.

Heading into the most recent international break, the Blades were looking for a good result against Charlton Athletic to strengthen the mood around the place even more, but one outcome Wilder has since described as a 'hammer blow' ensued.

Football League World has asked AI to predict the 2027/28 EFL Championship table if Manchester United and Manchester City were in it

Sheffield United would fall to a 2-1 defeat at the hands of Charlton, courtesy of goals from Millenic Alli and Matty Godden, but the bigger talking point from that game was the injury to Femi Seriki, who is set to face up to a year on the sidelines after sustaining a serious knee injury.

Seriki, 24, joined the Blades in 2019 from Bury after the Greater Manchester outfit fell into liquidation, and from there, the defender progressed through the Blades' ranks to the first team.

Spells on loan with Beerschot, Boston United, Rochdale, and Rotherham United would propel him into the first team fold in the 2024/25 campaign, where he has since gone on to make 78 appearances across all competitions for the club.

Out of contract at the end of the season, Seriki is yet to commit his future in South Yorkshire, as Football League World has taken a look at two Championship clubs that should be looking to pick up a bargain next summer.

By the time Seriki becomes a free agent, assuming he doesn't extend his stay with Sheffield United, Birmingham City will be hoping to call themselves a Premier League club once again.

Under head coach Chris Davies, the Blues have broken the EFL points record on their way to the Championship from League One, solidified themselves in the division, and now are looking towards the top two automatic spots this campaign.

Their current right-back options consist of Ethan Laird, Bright Osayi-Samuel, Taylor Gardner-Hickman, and Tomoki Iwata, though the latter two are expected to leave at the end of the current campaign when their contracts come to an end.

Neither Laird nor Osayi-Samuel has been able to nail down a consistent spot in the Blues' starting XI this season, as despite Osayi-Samuel impressing, Laird was picked ahead of the Nigerian for the club's crucial clash away to Stoke City.

In any scenario, a new permanent option in that position that is capable of making the step up to the Premier League must be sought after, and Seriki could be the perfect fit.

Although he won't be fit until around this time next year, meaning he will have no pre-season under his belt, there is no denying his quality, and in the Second City, he could take his game to the next level.

On a free transfer, this is a gamble Blues simply cannot ignore, and they must ensure they get themselves to the front of the queue this summer.

Where do you think Seriki should go if he were to leave Sheffield United? Would you like to see him at your club? Share your thoughts below!

Southampton, like Birmingham, will hope to be in the Premier League once again by the time Seriki's deal with the Blades expires, having climbed their way from -4 points and into promotion contention in the first third of the campaign.

Under Tonda Eckert, the Saints have proven themselves to be one of the best teams in the Championship over the past calendar year, and their meteoric rise up the table will have come as little surprise to anyone.

At right-back, James Bree has been amongst Eckert's most-used players at St Mary's since his appointment, having recalled the defender from his loan at Charlton Athletic in January 2026 and has been a mainstay in that spot ever since.

However, behind Bree, there is no obvious backup, and at 28, he will need replacing eventually; though Seriki won't be able to deputise for a bit, he could be the long-term heir at right-back at St Mary's.

Whether or not the Saints are promoted, they would be remiss to turn their nose up at the prospect of Seriki on a free transfer, as if they can get him back to full fitness in around 12 months' time, he could be an incredibly useful asset.

#2035. ‘Not Manchester United standard’, Paul Merson raises concerns over Manchester United squad

Shumail Sajid writes about Manchester United for Read Man Utd and Crystal Palace for Read Crystal Palace, with occasional pieces on other Premier League clubs. He has also written for FanSided's Red Devils Dispatch, Yardbarker, Anfield Central and The Sports Side.

Manchester United have failed to hit the numbers expected off them after a lackluster campaign so far.

Michael Carrick was relieved off his duties after winning just 1 game in his first 10, while collecting only 8 points. Manchester United arr currently languishing in the relegation spots and Carrick’s successor, Mauricio Pochettino, has a massive task ahead.

Manchester United have been leaky in defence and haven’t gone a game without conceding a goal this season. Their attacking returns are equally disappointing with United failing to convert chances regularly.

Paul Merson believes Manchester United must strengthen their defence in January but insists their problems extend beyond the backline, with concerns over their midfield and attacking options also needing attention.

The January transfer window could be the first stop for Pochettino for some shopping but the budget given to him as per a previous report by readmanutd isn’t much to make a difference.

Paul Merson believes the club have several areas to improve rather than focusing only on their defence.

Speaking on Sky Sports, the former Arsenal midfielder made it clear that United need to bring in defensive reinforcements.

“Manchester United will have to get centre-halves in, defenders in and full-backs in,” Merson said.

However, Merson does not believe defensive recruitment alone will solve United’s problems. He also questioned the team’s ability to control games in midfield and expressed concerns about the quality of their attacking options.

“I wouldn’t say that’s just been the problem. I don’t think they’ve got legs in midfield, I don’t think they’re dominating games in midfield,” he explained.

He was also critical of United’s forward line, suggesting that the current attacking options are not consistently performing.

“I’ve never really been a massive fan of their front three. I think they’re not Manchester United standard, in my opinion.”

Merson also compared the current generation with some of the club’s former greats, including Wayne Rooney, Ruud van Nistelrooy, Roy Keane, Paul Scholes, David Beckham and Cristiano Ronaldo. He compared players’ consistency with those earlier.

“Back in the day when it’s Rooney and them kind of players and Van Nistelrooy and Keane and Scholes and Beckham and Ronaldo, they were seven, eight out of ten every week. There wasn’t a four out of ten and a nine out of ten.”

“And if they have a four the week after, it doesn’t really matter. So for me, it hasn’t just been the defence.”

United could face difficult decisions when the transfer window opens, particularly if they want to strengthen multiple areas of the squad and with the budget available to Pochettino, that doesn’t seem to be the case.

#2034. Middlesbrough backed to offload £1m star amid 'strange' situation

Middlesbrough have been backed to potentially offload Leo Castledine from their Championship squad in January, with the highly-rated playmaker's time at the Riverside Stadium proving to be one of frustration so far.

The Reds are, again, pushing for promotion to the Premier League in what is Kim Hellberg's first full campaign on Teesside, having gone agonisingly close on two counts last term.

In an attempt to rectify glaringly obvious issues, particularly at the top end of the pitch, Steve Gibson heavily backed the Swede to recruit the likes of Max Arfsten, Rokas Pukstas, Myles Peart-Harris, Amario Cozier-Duberry, Will Lankshear and Kyle Joseph all within a remarkable summer of spending.

Such depth in the attacking areas has pushed Castledine's nose out of joint, with the former Chelsea academy graduate already struggling for minutes since his permanent switch from Stamford Bridge in January.

At 21, there are still many years to go in the playmaker's senior career, but it is fair to say that those in the North East are yet to see exactly why he earned rave reviews on loan at League One promotion hopefuls, Huddersfield Town, in the first half of last season.

Castledine scored 32 goals in 96 appearances for Chelsea's Under-18s and Under-21s sides, and now has experience in all of the Championship, League One and League Two, with a spell at Shrewsbury Town coming in the 2024/25 campaign.

10 goals in just 23 appearances for Huddersfield showcased the attacker's ability was a cut above most third tier counterparts, but despite impressing in his first nine second tier outings for Middlesbrough last season, Castledine has been utilised more so as a squad player this term.

His only start came on the opening day against Lincoln City, and he has since been sparsely used as a substitute, despite receiving a warning from Hellberg that he must be ready whenever called upon, with a full squad effort required if Boro are to end a 10-year hiatus from the Premier League.

Boro paid approximately £1m for the youngster's services in January on a four-and-a-half year contract, meaning Castledine will still have three years left to run on his deal by the time this season draws to a close.

In the short-term, Football League World's Middlesbrough fan pundit, Liam Day, believes that Hellberg's recent decision to bring Luke Ayling into midfield in place of Sebastian Berhalter, instead of pushing Peart-Harris into a deeper role and allowing Castledine to play as the '10' instead of on the left flank when he replaced Tommy Conway against Bristol City, only emphasised why a loan agreement makes sense.

"I feel like it's fairly obvious; Leo Castledine needs minutes," he told FLW.

"He was meant to have a big season. Kim Helberg even said in pre-season that if he's not playing 'I'd be very, very surprised'.

"I don't really know what's going on with him. Hellberg made the decision to bring Luke Ayling on in midfield over Castledine. It was a strange one," Day admitted.

"He could have very easily moved Peart-Harris back and put Castledine behind the striker, but he didn't. So, I think that shows.

"He obviously did get a bit of a cameo, but the fact Luke Ayling's coming on over him in midfield shows where he is in the packing order.

Boro fans, which clubs should look to loan in Leo Castledine this January? Comment below!

"I think Castledine probably needs a loan, which is a shame because when we bought him, I was very excited. I still think he's got quite a bit of potential, but a loan to a Championship team lower down or maybe a top-end League One club, and I think you're doing quite well," he claimed.

"I think Leo Castledine, probably, is quite desperate to get out as well, so I think it just makes sense for all parties."

Naturally, the chance to remain a part of a Middlesbrough squad which could go down in history would appeal to many players, and Castledine would have hoped for more opportunities to leave his mark than there have been for him in recent months.

As such, it feels inevitable that a loan move may be sanctioned, even if he is being favoured as a back-up option instead of previous Championship promotion winner, Jeremy Sarmiento, at this particular moment.

These four players need a fresh start away from Middlesbrough in January, whether that be on loan, permanently, or by having their loans cancelled

A return to form could be a win-win for Boro, especially if they are promoted, as they could still land a chance of receiving a profit on the playmaker's services if a permanent bidding war arose next summer.

Manchester United are reportedly leaning towards allowing Lisandro Martinez to leave next summer, with the club increasingly doubtful about extending the defender’s contract beyond the current season.

According to GIVEMESPORT journalist Ben Jacobs, Manchester United are not expected to activate the one-year extension included in Martinez’s deal. The Argentine’s contract expires next summer, although the club retain the option to keep him until 2028.

The situation is surprising given United’s ongoing problems at the back. They have struggled to find consistency in defence, with Matthijs de Ligt still working towards full match sharpness, Leny Yoro continuing his development and Harry Maguire struggling for regular opportunities. In the latest development, Ayden Heaven is also leaning towards going on a loan to secure regular minutes as he finds limited opportunities at United.

The 28-year-old arrived from Ajax in 2022 for an initial £56.7 million but has suffered two serious ACL injuries during his time at Old Trafford. His performances have also come under scrutiny this season, adding further uncertainty to his future.

Speaking on the Market Madness podcast, Jacobs suggested that Manchester United are already considering a defensive rebuild ahead of next summer.

“I think the Lisandro Martinez direction of travel is a departure, and there is the option to extend by one year. But my gut says that Manchester United, even if they can’t get defenders in the winter, will add further in the summer,” Jacobs said.

Jacobs also suggested that activating Martinez’s extension would not necessarily mean the club intend to keep him.

“Even if Man United extend the contract, that might just be a protection so they can still sell him,” he added.

Although the decision is not yet final but Manchester United are leaning towards letting Martinez go. They find themselves in a difficult place as far as their defensive cover is concerned. Despite their shortage of reliable defenders, the club appears increasingly open to moving on from the Argentine.

#2030. The last 7 permanent Sheffield Wednesday managers ranked from worst to best

Sheffield Wednesday have certainly been through their trials and tribulations in the last few years, but one thing they haven't done much of, unlike other clubs, is change managers every year.

Admittedly, there's still been some appointments that will have been seen now as mistakes, especially by former owner Dejphon Chansiri, but under their newest boss Dave Challinor, the good times may be coming back - at least that's the hope and expectation anyway now in League One.

But who have been the best and the worst of the Owls' last SEVEN permanent figures in the Hillsborough dugout? FLW ranks them all...

There was only ever going to be one manager that was the bottom of this list, and it's the absolute disaster of an appointment that was Xisco Munoz.

The feeling from Darren Moore's departure after their 2023 League One play-off final win was still leaving a sour taste in the mouths of Wednesday fans, with Chansiri having a very public spat with the previous boss, claiming he made unreasonable contract demands after leading the club back to the Championship.

Enter Xisco, who had already achieved promotion to the Premier League with Watford, but that was with a squad that was littered with top flight quality like Ismaila Sarr and Joao Pedro - Wednesday did not have that.

Added on was the fact he'd had indifferent stints with Huesca and Anorthosis since his departure from Vicarage Road. The end result? 12 games as Sheffield Wednesday manager, zero wins, four draws and eight losses.

The only permanent manager to never win a match for Wednesday after being sacked early on in the 2023-24 season, Xisco goes down in Owls folklore - for all the wrong reasons.

By the time he was appointed in November 2020, Tony Pulis had seen a lot in the game, with two promotions on his CV and a Premier League Manager of the Season award six years prior for the job he did with Crystal Palace.

He'd not managed for a year and a half though since his 2019 departure from Middlesbrough, and the rustiness was evident from when he set foot in the door at S6.

Breaking a record after eight matches in charge for the worst start to a Wednesday managerial reign in history, Pulis finally got a win at the ninth time of asking against Coventry City, but one match later, Pulis was sacked after just over a month in charge, with disagreements over transfer policy ahead of the January window opening being the primary reason.

Dave Challinor has hinted that Ernie Weaver could be leaving the club on loan soon. These five players should follow suit

It was a short stint at Hillsborough for the Welshman, but his reign didn't help the club's eventual drop into League One.

History will see Henrik Pedersen go down as a brave head coach of Sheffield Wednesday, given he stepped into the role with a squad that was incredibly undercooked for Championship level.

Pedersen stepped up after Danny Rohl's departure at a time where the Owls were in crisis mode when it came to their finances, and they were pretty much doomed from the moment a ball was kicked - let alone in October 2025 when Chansiri put them into administration.

In reality, Pedersen did well to actually get Wednesday to zero points when it was all said and done, with Arise Capital Partners opting to stick with him and not twist ahead of their 2026-27 League One campaign.

More criticisms though began to emerge of Pedersen in terms of his management and tactical ability in recent months, and despite scoring 12 goals combined past Bromley and AFC Wimbledon, back-to-back defeats against Notts County and Doncaster Rovers ultimately led to the Dane's departure in late October.

With just a 15 per cent win record, it's hard to rank Pedersen too highly, despite the circumstances he had to manage under, but he at least went down on his sword playing how he believed in.

Once upon a time, Garry Monk was highly-rated as a manager, having been given a chance at Swansea City whilst they were in the Premier League, and he landed a number of Championship jobs after that at Leeds United, Middlesbrough and Birmingham.

Taking over at Wednesday in September 2019, just a couple of months after his exit from St. Andrew's due to a breakdown of his relationship with the Blues board, Monk's first season at the club saw Wednesday finish 16th, which was a backwards step from 12th in 2018-19.

However, the poor start to 2020-21, which saw the Owls not leave the relegation zone in the first 11 matches, contributed to Monk's dismissal in November 2020, with a win percentage of just 31.08, he was only a slight bit better than Pulis, with an average 2019-20 season perhaps saving him from being remembered as really poor.

A very good player and manager at his peak in both professions, Steve Bruce ended up at Sheffield Wednesday in January 2019 to succeed Jus Luhukay with a point to prove, having been sacked by Aston Villa a few months prior.

His failure to get Villa back to the Premier League was a bit of a stain on his record, but it's one that had four promotion on it too, and Wednesday gambled on him getting a tune out of the squad.

In his half-season at Hillsborough, Bruce led Wednesday to seven wins from his 18 matches in charge, which included an 11-match unbeaten run in the Championship to eventually finish in 12th position.

Unfortunately for Wednesday, that impressed Newcastle United of the Premier League, and the allure of St. James Park was too much for Bruce to turn down - and the Magpies' approach for the veteran boss drew ire from the powers-that-be in S6, with legal action considered at the time.

It was a short appointment and a controversial departure, but you can't argue that Bruce got a lot out of his squad in his brief time in charge.

Following Tony Pulis' sacking, it took Wednesday over two months to get a new permanent manager, with Neil Thompson filling in in the interim, and it was Darren Moore who was next to take on the job - leaving a safe job at Doncaster Rovers in League One, where he was in the third tier play-off spots, for a Championship relegation battle at Hillsborough.

Wednesday were 23rd upon Moore's arrival, but losing his first three matches in charge did nothing to arrest the slide, and despite picking up three victories under his management (albeit he had to spend time away from the dugout due to a pneumonia diagnosis), the South Yorkshire outfit were relegated on the final day of the campaign.

League One was perhaps tougher than anticipated for Moore, whose Wednesday side were dumped out of the play-offs in 2021-22 by Sunderland at the semi-finals stage, despite winning 85 points in the regular season, but a year later, they made it to the final after overcoming a 4-0 first leg deficit against Peterborough United, thanks to a 5-1 scoreline on the night in the second leg and then a penalty shootout win.

Moore's time at the Owls ended on a high on the pitch with a play-off final win over county rivals Barnsley, but he was to surprisingly depart a month later with a 51 per cent win rate, due to the aforementioned spat with Chansiri - Moore claimed it was due to transfer policy, and he wouldn't be the first manager in the club's history to have not agreed with the Thai businessman on that.

Sheffield Wednesday already looked doomed in October 2023 thanks to the after-effects of Xisco Munoz's management, and instead of going for the tried and tested, Chansiri instead opted for a complete managerial novice in Danny Rohl.

The German coach had been an assistant at the likes of RB Leipzig, Bayern Munich, Southampton and the German national team before accepting Wednesday's offer, and he managed to mastermind a survival effort, pulling out of the drop zone in April before securing safety on the final day of 2023-24.

More progress was made in Rohl's first full season in 2024-25, with a 12th-placed finish achieved despite spending very little money on new players, aside from Ike Ugbo (that one didn't go well), and naturally, attention started to come from other clubs.

Is Danny Rohl's Sheffield Wednesday's best manager in recent times? Comment below!

What was also happening behind the scenes in 2025 with Chansiri's financial struggles was starting to cause a strain between Rohl and the club - he wasn't present for the start of pre-season training, and despite eventually turning up in mid-July, he left the club two weeks later because of their situation.

It wouldn't take long for Rohl to get back into work, landing a big job with Rangers just two months later, and he then upped sticks and left this past summer for Red Bull Salzburg - despite having a relatively safe job at Ibrox even with a third-placed finish in the Scottish Premiership.

For his first management job in football though, Rohl did very well with Wednesday - a 38 per cent win record perhaps doesn't tell the whole story with that one.

In the absence of any sort of goalscoring form from our strikers, Souček would seem like one of the most likely sources of goals in a team which has gone from being free-scoring and among the top goalscorers in the division to one that struggles to do anything other than hit the woodwork.

He’s a European trophy winner, an international player, a proven Premier League goalscorer and more than capable of scoring goals in the Championship.

#2027. Mauricio Pochettino proud of Man Utd response after chaotic Sporting draw

Shumail Sajid writes about Manchester United for Read Man Utd and Crystal Palace for Read Crystal Palace, with occasional pieces on other Premier League clubs. He has also written for FanSided's Red Devils Dispatch, Yardbarker, Anfield Central and The Sports Side.

Mauricio Pochettino praised Manchester United’s character and spirit after his side earned a 2-2 draw against Sporting Lisbon in the Champions League on Wednesday night.

Manchester United travelled to Portugal looking to respond after their disappointing 4-0 defeat to Liverpool in Pochettino’s first game in charge. They showed a much-improved performance away from home, although a number of costly moments prevented the new head coach from celebrating his first victory.

Bruno Fernandes scored twice on his return to the stadium, putting United ahead after Luis Suarez had given Sporting the lead. The home striker also scored twice, including a penalty, to ensure the points were shared.

Senne Lammens had earlier saved a Suarez spot-kick, but the United goalkeeper was involved in another penalty incident that allowed the Sporting forward to find the net. United also had two goals ruled out, while Youri Tielemans was sent off late in the contest.

Despite the frustrating outcome, Pochettino was pleased with what he saw from his players.

The Argentine felt United controlled large periods of the first half but were disappointed to go into the break behind.

“The first half I think we controlled the game, I think we dominated. We were disappointed to finish the first half 1-0 down,” Pochettino said after the game.

“The second half I think we started the way we want to play. That is the style, the character. That is the way we want to establish and feeling this way we can perform.”

The United boss also made it clear that he was proud of the players despite the decisions and incidents that went against them.

“I’m so proud of my players. I think it was a very tough game. I liked the team during 90 minutes, in the way that we showed personality and character.”

Pochettino felt his side had been punished repeatedly in important moments.

“In the second half, we recovered a lot of balls in the opposite half. We were aggressive and I think that is the way we want to play,” he added.

After the heavy defeat at Anfield, United showed a different level of fight in Lisbon. The draw will still feel like a missed opportunity for Manchester United and Pochettino. However, the Argentine manager believes his players are beginning to embrace the style of play he wants.

#2026. Rio Ferdinand once named the former EFL striker he hated facing

England legend Rio Ferdinand has been asked about the player that he feared playing against the most, and his reply might surprise some people.

Over the course of a glittering twenty-year playing career in which he played more than 700 games, Rio Ferdinand reached the absolute pinnacle of the game. He won the Premier League six times, and played in three Champions League finals, as well as five FA Cup and League Cup finals, while he also made 81 appearances for England and was selected to play in four consecutive World Cup finals squads.

Ferdinand has played both with and against some of the most-feted players of the 21st century in that time, but when questioned about the most difficult opponent that he had to play against over the course of his career, the answer he gave was an extremely surprising one; the former Southampton and Bolton Wanderers striker Kevin Davies.

As reported by Football365, Rio Ferdinand was speaking to the Beautiful Game podcast when he made his revelation. Asked about the player that he feared the most as a player himself, Ferdinand replied: "One of my hardest strikers to play against when people ask me - other than the ones that are obvious, like Ronaldo and Messi - was Kevin Davies."

Ferdinand confirmed that he is aware of the extent to which this is a surprising choice, but that it was Davies' physicality as a player which made him so difficult to play against: "You would never expect that, but he was always tough to play against for me, always caused me the most problems. He always was physical, just obstructing you all the time."

What are your recollections of Kevin Davies as a player? Let us know in the comments below!

The former West Ham and Manchester United star revealed that his teammate Nemanja Vidic had similar issues with the Liverpool striker Fernando Torres: "The ball might be over there [away from you] but he’s grabbing you and all this stuff. So you would never expect that, but Torres would have been that for Nemanja, probably." And he confirmed that he never had similar issues with Torres to those that he had with the former Bolton Wanderers striker: "With me one-v-one, he didn’t cause me any problems, if I’m honest. That’s just the way it is."

The Trotters cult icon spent just one season at Ewood Park, one that few will have good memories of.

If Rio Ferdinand was bothered by having to play against Kevin Davies in the Premier League, it should also be added that he was fairly successful at preventing the former Southampton and Bolton Wanderers striker from scoring against him.

According to Statmuse. Davies played against Rio Ferdinand 19 times throughout his career, but only recorded two goals and one assist in those matches. Those goals came nine years apart. Davies scored in his first appearance against Ferdinand, for Southampton against West Ham United in April 1997, and then for Bolton against Manchester United in April 2006.

Davies was renowned for his physical style of play, and it was far from universally popular with opposing players and managers. One of his more vocal critics was Ferdinand's manager throughout his time at Old Trafford, Sir Alex Ferguson, who said of Davies in 2008, "[the then-Bolton manager] Gary Megson came out and defended Kevin Davies, but it's hard to defend him when he makes tackles like he did last week." This came a week after a challenge by Davies on Arsenal's Gael Clichy had led to an enforced substitution and X-ray checks on Clichy's shin.

Bolton's aggressive style of play had been introduced by Sam Allardyce, who sought to maximise the playing resources at his disposal through playing direct football. "We got heavily criticised at the time," Allardyce told BBC Sport in 2025. "But we were ahead of the game and lots of people, particularly at the bigger clubs, or even the press, were not too complimentary."

But it was effective. Davies was at Bolton for ten years, of which nine were spent in the Premier League, and although he only managed to get into double-figures in terms of goalscoring once, he was a part of a Bolton team which managed eleven consecutive seasons of Premier League football at the start of this century. In his 2017 book about the tactics of the Premier League era, The Mixer, writer Michael Cox said of Davies that, "He essentially turned matches into a stop-start scrap based around dead-ball situations, which suited Bolton perfectly."

Rio Ferdinand played against some of the greatest players of all-time, and there's no doubt that Messi and Ronaldo were more skilled players than Kevin Davies. But the very fact that Davies was the first name to spring to mind when Ferdinand was asked about his "toughest" opponent suggests that, when players think of that word, they think immediately of the one most likely to hurt them physically beyond any other considerations.

#2024. Pochettino fumes at ‘impossible’ decisions after Man Utd draw with Sporting

Shumail Sajid writes about Manchester United for Read Man Utd and Crystal Palace for Read Crystal Palace, with occasional pieces on other Premier League clubs. He has also written for FanSided's Red Devils Dispatch, Yardbarker, Anfield Central and The Sports Side.

Mauricio Pochettino was left frustrated by several refereeing decisions during Manchester United’s 2-2 draw with Sporting Lisbon, insisting his side were punished in key moments of the game.

Manchester United had to settle for a point in Portugal after a chaotic evening away from home. Bruno Fernandes scored twice, but Luis Suarez also found the net on two occasions to deny Pochettino his first win as United head coach.

Referee Szymon Marciniak came under scrutiny for a series of controversial decisions. He ruled out an Amad Diallo goal after penalising Youri Tielemans for a foul in the build-up, blowing his whistle before the ball crossed the line. That meant VAR could not intervene on the goal and it was not given.

The Polish official also awarded Sporting a first-half penalty and disallowed what would have been a late United winner. He blew whistle on Patrick Dorgu for pushing goalkeeper Kaique Pereira, disallowing the goal.

Pochettino did not hide his frustration when asked about the decisions after the match.

“I think your first question is difficult to answer because I think everyone knows all that was, it was impossible,” he said after the game.

“You know, it’s difficult to understand why that happened on the field. It’s difficult to find a game where you get punished [so much] in one game. We were punished a lot in key actions.”

United also conceded an 80th-minute equaliser after Senne Lammens failed to hold a cross, allowing Suarez to score from close range.

However, Pochettino was keen to defend his goalkeeper rather than blame him for the mistake.

“I think, please, it’s to blame us,” the United boss said.

He acknowledged that his side needed to manage such situations better.

“But of course, we need to accept, we accept the challenge and we are here to try to improve, you know, the small details that for sure we will improve.”

Pochettino’s frustration was understandable after two similar incidents of bad refereeing in his first two games at United. Leny Yoro’s red card against Liverpool was later overturned on appeal, while a series of errors against Sporting cost him yet another victory. But despite the errors, Pochettino also recognises that his players need to improve their decision-making during games.

The London Stadium is a tough venue to fill for West Ham given its huge capacity, even when everything is going well. Therefore, there was always likely to be a reduced attendance against Stoke City on Saturday anyway, given the Hammers’ recent performances and results.

But it looks set to get considerably worse, with many of those using public transport to get to the stadium facing significant disruption.

Essex and Shenfield: National Rail has confirmed disruption to Greater Anglia services, with replacement buses connecting passengers to the Central line at Newbury Park.

Lea Bridge: Engineering works mean Hertford East services normally terminating at Stratford will be diverted to Liverpool Street. There will also be no trains between Meridian Water and Stratford.

There will be no Elizabeth line services through central London due to additional engineering works, although Stratford station itself remains open.

Supporters can also consult West Ham’s official stadium travel guide, which includes information on accessible shuttle buses.

#2021. What Kim Hellberg told Finn Azaz on the pitch after Middlesbrough flashpoint

Middlesbrough boss Kim Hellberg has revealed he told Southampton’s Finn Azaz he had a responsibility to ‘do better’ after his controversial celebration in Saints' 2-0 win on Friday night.

There was a lot of hype going into the fixture after the south coast side had been expelled from the play-offs last season for spying on Boro’s training sessions in the build up to the semi-final.

With the two clubs now battling for promotion once again, it promised to be a ferocious atmosphere at St. Mary’s Stadium when they met - and it’s fair to say it delivered on that front, as Tonda Eckert’s side ran out winners.

Another sub-plot to the game was Azaz coming up against his former club, after the attacking midfielder left Boro to join Saints in the summer of 2025.

Of course, this wasn’t the first time he had played against his former club, but it was the first time he had got on the scoresheet, and, after slotting home following a mistake from Aiden Morris, Azaz only had one thing on his mind.

Despite scoring in front of the home end, in a celebration similar to Emmanuel Adebayor against Arsenal for Man City, the Irish international turned and ran straight towards the away end.

As he got closer, Azaz mimicked a crying gesture to the Boro fans, and it started a melee on the pitch, as Will Lankshear initially had a go at the Saints man on the pitch before players from both sides got involved.

Who has the best and worst average attendances in the Championship so far this season? Football League World takes a look...

Obviously, it was a celebration that angered Boro fans, but, speaking after the game, Azaz insisted he had ‘no regrets’ as he claimed that they had abused him and his family, both last night and in the previous campaign.

Naturally, the celebration was a talking point, and Hellberg could be seen in discussion with Azaz on the pitch at full-time, and the Boro chief confirmed to Teesside Live that he told the 26-year-old he shouldn’t have celebrated in the manner he did.

“With Finn Azaz, I told him, ‘I think you have to do better, you cannot do things like that’. That was a key thing to tell him.

“I know it's a lot of emotions and I know emotions can get the better of you, but that's what I told him, ‘you have to be better on that occasion. Like I said to him, it wasn't a good move, but players are young people and emotions come into it, but you can handle it and should handle it in a better way.”

You can understand both sides to this, as, from a professional perspective, Hellberg is right. This game is already high on tension, so it’s not sensible for Azaz to antagonise the Boro supporters further.

Yet, from a human perspective, everyone can see why Azaz reacted in the way he did if his family was getting abused, and fans shouldn’t complain if a player gives a bit back.

What did you make of Finn Azaz's celebration? Let us know in the comments below.

So, it’s one that may divide opinion, but the reality is that it has added another layer to this new rivalry, and Azaz is certain to get pelters when he returns to the Riverside Stadium with Southampton in March.

That promises to be another great occasion, and, given the quality both teams displayed last night, it’s a fixture that is likely to have major implications in the promotion race.

#2020. Bruno Fernandes tells players what to do next after Sporting draw

Shumail Sajid writes about Manchester United for Read Man Utd and Crystal Palace for Read Crystal Palace, with occasional pieces on other Premier League clubs. He has also written for FanSided's Red Devils Dispatch, Yardbarker, Anfield Central and The Sports Side.

Bruno Fernandes has urged Manchester United to stick together and fight for their season after they were held to a 2-2 draw by Sporting Lisbon in the Champions League.

The United captain scored twice on his return to the stadium, putting Manchester United ahead after Luis Suarez had given Sporting the lead. The home striker also scored twice, including a penalty, to ensure the points were shared.

Senne Lammens had earlier saved a Suarez spot-kick, but the United goalkeeper was involved in another penalty incident that allowed the Sporting forward to find the net. United also had two goals ruled out after some controversial decisions, while Youri Tielemans was sent off late in the contest.

It was another frustrating result for United, who are still searching for their first win under Mauricio Pochettino. Fernandes believes there were positives in the performance, but insists the team must now focus on getting results.

Speaking to TNT Sports after the match, Fernandes revealed that Pochettino wanted his players to show more aggression after the break.

“[At half-time the manager] wanted more aggression. more bodies. The first goal comes from that.”

The Portuguese midfielder felt United had controlled much of the first half despite conceding. He admitted they needed more presence in the final third.

“Obviously, I think we started the game well. We gave a penalty away where Senne [Lammens] saved it. We gave one or two counters, but we were very good in recovery positions.

“They got the goal, but we were still in control of the game. We didn’t have much people in the last third. Second half we got the two goals. That was the moment we should push a bit more.”

United’s inability to hold on to their lead was another setback, but Fernandes refused to single out individuals for the mistakes.

“Mistakes are part of football and from that you get goals. Everyone has to take the blame for everything we do good and we do bad as well. We need to be together in the good and in the bad moments.”

“We need points to get through. and we need to focus on the next one. Now the moment is to get back to the Premier League. We need to stick together and fight for our lives.”

#2019. Chelsea World Cup Knockout Load Gives Xabi Alonso Pre-Season Problem

Chelsea’s World Cup contingent has moved from a group-stage watchlist into a genuine Xabi Alonso planning problem.

Chelsea’s own tournament update confirms that Enzo Fernandez, Mike Penders, Moises Caicedo, Kendry Paez, Malo Gusto and Jorrel Hato have reached the Round of 32.

England have also progressed after their final Group L win over Panama, which keeps Reece James and Trevoh Chalobah inside the wider knockout picture.

For supporters, that is a status marker. For Alonso, it is where summer pride starts to become pre-season compression.

The concern is not simply volume. It is where the minutes are landing.

Enzo has not missed a minute for Argentina, while Caicedo has remained central for Ecuador and captained them in the 2-1 win over Germany.

Those are not fringe workloads. They are the two midfield profiles Chelsea have built large parts of their control game around.

Alonso’s first Chelsea pre-season was always going to demand clarity through the middle of the pitch.

Instead, the players most central to that reset are still operating in knockout football.

Caicedo’s Ecuador role is the cleanest example. Read Chelsea has already assessed how his captaincy display against Germany strengthened his leadership case, but the next layer is more complicated.

Every additional knockout tie gives him more tournament rhythm, more authority and more fatigue.

Argentina’s route against Cape Verde keeps him on a glamorous stage at exactly the moment Chelsea need to settle his role, mood and tactical responsibilities under Alonso.

If Madrid-related noise continues around him, the club cannot afford a sluggish July handover.

Reece James started England’s first two matches before a hamstring issue ruled him out of the Panama game, according to the Guardian.

England still topped the group and moved into a last-32 tie with DR Congo, but James’ situation is exactly the kind of detail Chelsea’s medical team will monitor closely.

Chelsea have already had to plan around a large World Cup group.

The broader issue was clear in Read Chelsea’s earlier pre-season workload piece, but the knockout stage sharpens it because the returns will now be staggered.

Enzo brings a maximum group-stage load. Caicedo brings captaincy responsibility and heavy Ecuador minutes.

James brings knockout qualification mixed with another hamstring-management question.

Gusto and Hato remain tied to France and the Netherlands, while Penders and Paez are still absorbing tournament environments before club reintegration.

That is a spine issue, not a fringe issue.

Alonso needs automatisms in possession, spacing around the double pivot, clearer full-back behaviour and pressing triggers from midfield.

Those details do not bed in properly when key players arrive in drips after a major summer tournament.

Players returning from knockout football can bring competitive sharpness that closed-door friendlies cannot replicate.

Caicedo captaining Ecuador through pressure games matters. Enzo playing high-leverage minutes for Argentina matters.

Gusto and Hato absorbing tournament detail also helps Chelsea’s defensive reset.

But Chelsea cannot treat every tournament minute as clean preparation.

Alonso must decide who returns straight into tactical work, who needs a genuine pause and who can handle August without creating an avoidable injury bill by September.

That is where the James situation feels central.

If Chelsea’s captain carries a World Cup hamstring warning, the club’s right-sided structure becomes more than a selection debate.

It becomes an availability question that touches Gusto, the wider defensive rebuild and the need for control from midfield.

Read Chelsea has already looked at James’ captaincy test under Alonso, and the injury layer now makes that test sharper.

This is the hidden cost of a strong international footprint.

Chelsea want players good enough to survive deep into tournaments.

Alonso now has to make sure that status does not leave his first league weeks short of the very control those players are meant to provide.

#2018. Ashley Young tears into referee after Manchester United denied dramatic late winner

Shumail Sajid writes about Manchester United for Read Man Utd and Crystal Palace for Read Crystal Palace, with occasional pieces on other Premier League clubs. He has also written for FanSided's Red Devils Dispatch, Yardbarker, Anfield Central and The Sports Side.

Manchester United had to settle for a point in Portugal after a chaotic evening away from home.

Bruno Fernandes scored twice, but Luis Suarez also found the net on two occasions to deny Pochettino his first win as United head coach.

Referee Szymon Marciniak came under scrutiny for a series of controversial decisions. He ruled out an Amad Diallo goal after penalising Youri Tielemans for a foul in the build-up, blowing his whistle before the ball crossed the line. That meant VAR could not intervene on the goal and it was not given.

The Polish official also awarded Sporting a first-half penalty and disallowed what would have been a late United winner. He blew whistle on Patrick Dorgu for pushing goalkeeper Kaique Pereira, disallowing the goal.

The decisions left plenty of frustration among Manchester United supporters, but former footballer Ashley Young called the officiating disgraceful.

Young questioned several decisions made by Marciniak, particularly the disallowed Amad goal and the late incident involving Dorgu.

“The referee’s performance was just simply wow. The decisions that he gave, including the one for what should have been Amad’s equaliser, with Tielemans, were unbelievable,” Ashley Young said while talking to BBC.

“Tielemans getting booked, which should never have been a booking, and then eventually getting sent off later. It should have been an equalising goal.

“Then the third goal as well, which should have stood, because he’s saying there’s a foul, whether he’s saying Lisandro Martinez or Patrick Dorgu fouled the keeper. The keeper comes out and flaps at it before he’s even touched.

“How that has gone to VAR is beyond me. His decision-making today is nothing more than a disgrace.”

The disallowed goals proved particularly costly, with Pochettino’s side missing the chance to take all three points despite Fernandes’ brace.

Mauricio Pochettino is still without a win after replacing Michael Carrick. Manchester United faces Brentford next with a hope of a first win for Pochettino.

#2017. Malo Gusto’s Kante Lesson Gives Chelsea A £75m Xabi Alonso Decision

Malo Gusto’s World Cup has suddenly become more than a France subplot for Chelsea. It is now a live assessment of whether Xabi Alonso inherits a right-back worth protecting, reshaping or trading at the peak of his market.

Chelsea’s own interview with Gusto this week underlined the human part of that equation. The 23-year-old spoke about learning from N’Golo Kante, calling the former Blue one of the best midfielders France have produced and stressing the value of his example on and off the pitch.

That matters because Kante is not just a nostalgic reference point. He remains the standard Chelsea supporters still use when judging humility, intensity and reliability in a high-pressure dressing room.

For Gusto, those qualities arrive at a decisive moment. Reports around the player’s future claim Chelsea value him at around £75million, with the imminent Marco Palestra deal creating a more crowded full-back picture.

That number looks aggressive, but the logic is clear. Gusto is young, capped by France, under contract, Premier League-tested and capable of playing in several defensive structures.

🚨🚨| NEW: Chelsea are open to selling Malo Gusto this summer, with his agent already in 𝐓𝐀𝐋𝐊𝐒 with Manchester City and Inter. Chelsea will only sell if their valuation is met.{@siphillipssport} pic.twitter.com/vNR2bWud9F

The easiest reading of Gusto’s Kante comments is sentimental. It should not be.

For Alonso, who officially begins work on July 1, the important detail is what those comments say about the player Chelsea have been developing.

Gusto has not always looked completely settled at Stamford Bridge. His best games have carried thrust, speed and recovery power, while his less convincing spells have raised questions about final-ball quality and defensive concentration.

That uncertainty is exactly why the next coach matters.

Alonso’s previous teams have leaned heavily on wide players who can receive under pressure, attack space early and still protect the back line when possession breaks down. Gusto has the athletic base for that job.

The test is whether his decision-making can be refined enough to make him a structural piece rather than a rotation asset.

That is where the Kante reference lands with force. Chelsea do not need Gusto to imitate Kante’s position. They need him to absorb the same professional standard: repeat actions, clean defensive choices, no wasted emotion and total commitment to the collective rhythm.

The Marco Palestra deal changes the right side of Chelsea’s squad immediately. Read Chelsea has already examined how Palestra’s arrival offers a tactical clue over Alonso’s defensive plans, and that pressure is now sharpened by market noise around Gusto.

Chelsea can frame the situation in two ways.

One is profit-led. If a club comes close to the reported £75million level, selling a player signed from Lyon for a much lower fee becomes a powerful PSR lever.

The other is football-led. If Alonso sees Gusto as a high-upside wing-back who fits his model, selling him just as the coaching environment becomes more suitable would carry long-term risk.

The complication is Reece James. The captain’s fitness issues, including his current England hamstring concern, mean Chelsea still need genuine right-sided depth.

Palestra may be part of the future, but Gusto is already part of the present. Chelsea have too often needed emergency solutions in that area to treat proven depth lightly.

That is why Read Chelsea’s recent look at James awaiting hamstring scan results matters in this debate. Right-back remains one of the most talented areas of the squad, but also one of the least straightforward.

This is why Gusto’s France rhythm is more valuable than a simple tournament diary entry. Chelsea are watching a player operate inside an elite international camp, learn from a club legend and handle a public transfer valuation that can change his status overnight.

Alonso’s first decision does not have to be final, but it does have to be clear.

If Gusto stays, he needs a defined role early in pre-season and a pathway that makes sense alongside Palestra and James. If Chelsea sell, they need to do it at a number that justifies weakening one of the few squad areas where youth, speed and top-level experience already overlap.

Gusto’s Kante lesson, then, is not just a feel-good Chelsea connection. It is a reminder of the standard Alonso must demand before deciding whether £75million is a price to accept or a warning sign that Chelsea should hold firm.

#2016. Tonda Eckert 'angered' by Southampton actions as bizarre Kim Hellberg incident emerges

Tonda Eckert was not pleased with some of the actions behind the scenes at St. Mary's following his side winning 2-0 over Kim Hellberg's Middlesbrough on Friday night.

The fallout from Spygate was always going to mean a tense game between Southampton and Middlesbrough, but both look likely to be in the automatic promotion mix again this season, considering the depth and quality of the respective squads.

In the end, a tense game was settled in the second half. Ryan Manning put the hosts 1-0 up before Boro pushed for an equaliser. However, Aidan Morris' mistake handed Southampton all three points as Finn Azaz struck to make it 2-0 against his former side.

Prior to the match, the Southampton social media team were playing into the new rivalry emerging from the Spygate incident, which certainly ruffled a few feathers on Teesside.

Furthermore, Azaz ran the length of the pitch in Emmanuel Adebayor style to mock the Middlesbrough fans in the away end. He was booked for the incident but that wasn't the last moment of controversy between the clubs.

That said, not everyone was pleased with the way things were handled. Tonday Eckert, as per Jacob Tanswell of The Athletic, grabbed tissues from the press conference table. They were put there before he arrived and for Kim Hellberg's arrival. Eckert was angered by the video Southampton posted this morning and the tissues, too.

Tanswell claims it's such a poor look, with Hellberg upset at the back end of last season during the play-offs, and the Southampton decision to put the tissues in the press conference being a nod to that.

FLW have ranked the 10 best players in the EFL Championship for the 2026/27 season aged 22 or below, including a pair of Middlesbrough stars.

As shared by Boropolis on X (formerly Twitter), Eckert was questioned on a number of the incidents, stating: "It's a tough question because I don't want to go there. We can take this one off because, for me, there is nothing to ask."

Bobby Manzi of The Mail claims Eckert reminded his club to keep their 'class'. He also assured the media that none of the provocation came from him.

Hellberg and Eckert appear to have cleared the air privately via a phone call already, which perhaps explains his exasperation at the volume of moments to wind up Boro fans and attempts to do the same to the Swedish manager.

There was always going to be extra needle surrounding Middlesbrough's trip to Southampton, given the recent history between the clubs and the competitive stakes involved in the race for automatic promotion.

Both are ambitious sides with Premier League aspirations, and there is plenty of familiarity and rivalry between their respective fanbases. However, Southampton's media team and staff arguably added unnecessary fuel to the fire, turning what was already an intriguing fixture into an even more combustible occasion.

Rather than allowing the football to do the talking, their actions risked creating additional animosity and made an already significant Championship encounter even more heated. They also posted the image of Eckert and Hellberg above on X.

Speaking via Alfie House of The Daily Echo, Hellberg responded: "They tried to make this a final. They tried to fire everything up and it's tough trying to keep the class in those moments. I thought we had moved on but I have seen some of their posts trying to mock me. They are a good team, so there's no need."

Of course, the posts have not gone unnoticed on social media from Southampton supporters, Middlesbrough fans, nor neutrals either. The response has been vast, with one Chief football writer saying: "Agreed. An odd decision along with the video."

A further reply from a Southampton fan read: "Most of our fanbase also didn't like the video. Hope whoever signed off on it gets moved on."

What do you make of all the incidents? Comment your thoughts below!

Another Southampton supporter added: "Great performance on the pitch. Seemingly off it decision making, oversight and governance have a way to go"

Not all of the Southampton fanbase were against it, with another stating: "Grow up."

Shumail Sajid writes about Manchester United for Read Man Utd and Crystal Palace for Read Crystal Palace, with occasional pieces on other Premier League clubs. He has also written for FanSided's Red Devils Dispatch, Yardbarker, Anfield Central and The Sports Side.

Despite a slow start to last season, Bruno Fernandes went on to finish the last season with 21 Premier League assists, breaking the competition’s single-season record.

This season has been a different situation. He isn’t at his usual best, contract talks have reported stalled and he publicy questioned Carrick’s tactics.

Bruno Fernandes has come under criticism for his performances and Ashley Young joins in as the latest to call for Bruno’s sale in January.

Manchester United have been told to cash in on Bruno Fernandes in January rather than offer the midfielder another contract. Meanwhile, Young identifies Morgan Gibbs-White as an upgrade over the Portuguese star.

The criticism of Fernandes has been particularly strong, with questions raised over his influence in central midfield.

“If Manchester United can cash in on him in January, I’d do that. I wouldn’t be looking to extend his contract at all. Keep him there, he’d be unhappy,” Ashley Young said while talking to BBC.

Young also questioned Fernandes’ attitude towards individual recognition, suggesting that winning personal awards appears to be an important part to his United career.

“He seems to me as a player that personal accolades are more important than the team. And that’s what he’s about. He’ll be looking at that, yeah, I want player of the year. I won player of the year. It was, it was me. You know, it weren’t my other teammates.”

The concerns were not limited to Fernandes’ attitude. His defensive positioning and the spaces he leaves behind when playing in central midfield were also highlighted.

The criticism comes from a view that opponents have regularly found opportunities to play through United’s midfield, particularly when Fernandes steps forward.

“I was at Everton teams, playing against Manchester United, and if he’s playing in central midfield, the tactic was, play through the midfield when you see them step out because there’s so much space in there. And it’s been the theme. It’s been the theme for years that Manchester United, if they play him in central midfield, there’s spaces all behind him.”

Ashley Young’s suggested alternative is Nottingham Forest’s Morgan Gibbs-White, who is believed to offer a different balance to the United midfield.

“I would go and get Morgan Gibbs-White if you can. And I’d go and do it in January. For me, I think Morgan Gibbs-White would give more to that team than what Bruno Fernandes is now.”

It would be a major decision for United if they let him go. There is no doubt on his quality as he has scored 113 goals in 341 appearances since arriving from Sporting in 2020.

However, his future has become a talking point after United reportedly saw two contract offers rejected. Fernandes is understood to want a four-year agreement, while the club remain cautious about committing to such a deal with the midfielder already 32.

With Mauricio Pochettino in the dugout now and reportedly involved in his contract negotiations, the upcoming months can be very different for Manchester United and Bruno Fernandes.

#2014. Messi was a deity among Argentina’s unholy rabble

Little sorcerer calls time on playing for his country six weeks after World Cup final defeat which was marred by brutality of his team-mates

Oliver Brown leads coverage of the greatest events in sport all over the world. He has reported on multiple Olympic Games, World Cups, Ashes series and Super Bowls, plus all major golf and tennis tournaments. His awards include Sports Feature Writer of the Year and Sports Interviewer of the Year. He was named Sports Journalist of the Year in 2024 by the London Press Club. You can find him on X at @oliverbrown_tel.

Oliver Brown leads coverage of the greatest events in sport all over the world. He has reported on multiple Olympic Games, World Cups, Ashes series and Super Bowls, plus all major golf and tennis tournaments. His awards include Sports Feature Writer of the Year and Sports Interviewer of the Year. He was named Sports Journalist of the Year in 2024 by the London Press Club. You can find him on X at @oliverbrown_tel.

Lionel Messi’s haunted expression told you more than a three-page retirement statement, artfully displayed alongside a golden pen, ever could. Sobbing and desolate under a cloudless New Jersey sky, he understood that his last game for Argentina had also been among his worst.

Where four years earlier he had adorned the greatest World Cup final with two goals, he found no artistry to salvage this abomination of an encore, drifting into anonymity while his team-mates triggered a bare-knuckle brawl. No wonder he stood apart while Leandro Paredes and Nahuel Molina did their worst, preferring to absorb one more chorus of adoration from the blue-and-white disciples before forsaking the stage for good.

You could make the case that Messi, as captain of an unholy rabble that had sought only to kick lumps out of Spain, should have taken a moral lead by hauling his team-mates into line, rather than reducing himself to their level by agitating to have Marc Cucurella sent off.

And yet for 20 years, the little sorcerer stayed aloof from his nation’s most lurid antics on the pitch, establishing himself as a strangely beatific presence on whom the highest ideals could be projected. Anybody who has heard Messi’s name being chanted by 50,000 fervent Argentines would have felt it. He was as close as 21st-century sport has come to a secular deity, the object of such veneration that Pope Francis felt compelled to remind Catholics that it was sacrilegious to keep calling him God.

Today, with one agonised announcement, that glorious delirium is over, and already Argentina seems not to know what to do with itself. Pablo Giralt, a sports anchor in Buenos Aires, was unable even to speak when he heard the news live on air, while shattered young fans described how they had called their parents in tears.

Everybody had known the moment was approaching, given the finality of his exit from the final and the subsequent death of his father, Jorge, but it still triggered an unbearable sense of loss.

Messi was the force who galvanised a nation, propelling his side from the unfathomable low of defeat to Saudi Arabia at the 2022 World Cup to holding the trophy aloft 26 days later. Who could ever hope to emulate him, to detonate such joy that the team’s homecoming bus parade in the capital had to be abandoned for a helicopter ride because of the millions on the streets?

“Thank you, God, for making me Argentine,” Messi wrote in his earnest sign-off, his strength of allegiance unfailing to the end. As a veteran of 207 international matches, with his last at La Bombonera distinguished by an ecstatic ovation, he understood both the passions he unleashed among his people and the extent to which his own story became that of an entire country.

You struggled to imagine what life was like in the eye of this madness, with his every move stalked. For the wonder of Messi was that the cult went beyond borders, that the joy he inspired across six World Cups made him beloved to billions. An abiding memory of the 2022 final is of the walk back to the metro station in Doha, where thousands of Nepalese and Bangladeshi supporters, all part of the vast migrant workforce that had built the stadiums, united in “Messi, Messi” refrains even at 1am.

Messi was majestic at that tournament, so imperious in filleting Croatia in the semi-finals that Argentina’s TV reporters abandoned even the pretence of objectivity. “Truly, you made your mark in everyone’s life, and that to me is beyond winning any World Cup,” gushed Sofia Martinez of Television Publica. And when he won it all, the mark only deepened. To occupy any press box at the World Cup where Argentina were involved this summer was to see South American colleagues in “Messi 10” jerseys, helplessly in thrall to his greatness.

As a 39-year-old, he confounded every expectation, scoring a hat-trick against Algeria and breaking Miroslav Klose’s World Cup goals record. Even when engineering those implausible fightbacks against Egypt and England, he held a volatile team together with a minimum of fuss.

Lionel Messi: #FIFAWorldCup edition 🇦🇷🌟 pic.twitter.com/E2xOh3Iose

To study Messi at his last World Cup was to see a man spared the obligation to do anything off the ball. For large periods of each game, the most minutely scrutinised athlete on the planet would do little besides wander around, only to ignite when it mattered most. You saw it in the fateful semi-final with England, where, at 1-0 down, he sloped off to the right touchline as if absent-mindedly gardening. Except he was plotting his opponents’ downfall, working out the precise spots from which to unleash two sumptuous crosses and shatter English hearts.

That alchemy would elude him in the final, where Argentina’s bid for immortality brought only instant notoriety, not to mention £236,000 in fines for misconduct. Was Messi’s image hurt by his connection to the chaos? Not in the long run. Nobody likes to cling to the fact that Pelé’s swansong for Brazil was a drawn friendly with Yugoslavia, or that Diego Maradona bowed out of World Cup football by failing a drug test for ephedrine. What endure are the indelible masterpieces those players bequeathed en route.

It will be the same for Messi, a genius defined less by his ending than by the electrifying adrenalin rush he produced along the way, spanning three finals, 21 goals, and countless flourishes to take the breath away. “Thank you” was all he had left to say. And yet the gratitude, ultimately, is all ours.

Chelsea’s World Cup watch has moved beyond simple minutes management.

Senegal’s Round-of-32 meeting with Belgium now gives Xabi Alonso a live read on two very different development tracks.

Nicolas Jackson’s attacking authority is the immediate question. Mamadou Sarr’s defensive readiness is the longer-term one.

Chelsea confirmed that Senegal kept their knockout hopes alive with a 5-0 win over Iraq, with Jackson featuring from the bench.

Senegal have since moved into the knockouts, where they face Belgium in Seattle on Wednesday 1 July.

Jackson and Sarr travel into that game with contrasting club questions attached. Both still carry clear Chelsea relevance.

Sarr has not been the loudest Chelsea story of the tournament.

The 20-year-old is still moving through the awkward stage between prospect, squad option and saleable BlueCo asset.

Knockout football against Belgium can sharpen that picture quickly.
